name: Extract Function
tradeoff: Over-eager extraction can produce a maze of one-line functions; aim for extractions that earn their name with at least one decision or one transformation.
goal: Each function reads as a single named domain step — what it does, not how.
savings: Calling code becomes a sequence of named intentions; bugs concentrate inside the now-named subroutines.

name: Inline Function
tradeoff: If the function had a meaningful name covering several call sites, inlining can scatter the intent — only inline when the body is as clear as the wrapper.
goal: Trivial wrappers vanish; the call site reads as exactly what's happening.
savings: One fewer indirection to follow when reading; smaller surface to maintain.

name: Extract Variable
tradeoff: Over-extracting tiny expressions clutters scope with one-shot names; extract when the expression carries domain meaning the surrounding code can't speak.
goal: A complex expression earns a name that says what it represents in the domain.
savings: Reusable in nearby code; debugging shows the intermediate value; comments explaining the expression become unnecessary.
before: if (order.qty * order.price - Math.max(0, order.qty - 500) * order.price * 0.05 > 1000) { /* ... */ }

name: Inline Variable
tradeoff: Inlining a name that did carry domain meaning costs readability — only inline when the expression is already self-explanatory.
goal: Single-use variables that just rename their right-hand side disappear; the expression speaks for itself.
savings: Less local clutter, fewer redundant names, smaller scopes to track.
before:
const basePrice = order.basePrice;
return basePrice > 1000;
after: return order.basePrice > 1000;

name: Change Function Declaration
tradeoff: Mass renames or signature shifts ripple to every caller; refactor in tooling-supported steps and update tests with each batch.
goal: Function names match what they actually do; parameter lists carry only what the function needs, in the order callers expect.
savings: Call sites read fluently; mismatches between expectation and behavior surface immediately at the boundary.

name: Encapsulate Variable
tradeoff: Adds a layer of indirection that pays off only when every access goes through the wrapper — leakage of direct access undoes the benefit.
goal: All reads and writes pass through a small named function that owns validation, logging, and invariants.
savings: A bug fix or audit becomes a one-line addition inside the wrapper; consumers never need to change.
before: let defaultOwner = { firstName: 'Martin', lastName: 'Fowler' };

name: Rename Variable
tradeoff: A rename is small but cross-file; ensure your tooling catches every reference (including string templates and comments).
goal: Variable names match the domain role they play, not their implementation type or scratch nature.
savings: Reading the variable's name tells you everything you need without checking its definition.
before: const a = height * width;
after: const area = height * width;

name: Introduce Parameter Object
tradeoff: Premature parameter objects hide which fields are actually needed by which method — wait until the clump appears in 3+ places before extracting.
goal: Related arguments travel together as one well-named value object that the function (and callers) refer to by name.
savings: Adding a related field is one type change instead of touching every call site; intent is named.

name: Combine Functions into Class
tradeoff: Wrapping passive data in a class that nobody else uses adds ceremony — only combine when 2+ functions take the same data and would benefit from co-located behavior.
goal: Functions that all act on the same data live alongside it as methods; calls become method calls on a domain object.
savings: Encapsulation tightens; tests target the class; new operations land in one obvious place.
before:
function baseCharge(reading)    { /* uses reading */ }
function taxableCharge(reading) { /* uses reading */ }

name: Combine Functions into Transform
tradeoff: Building a transform up-front when only one derivation exists is BDUF — wait for the second derivation before introducing the transform.
goal: Multiple derived values from the same source come from one transform that produces an enriched record.
savings: Derivations stay consistent (no two callers compute slightly different versions); cache invalidation becomes obvious.
before:
function base(reading)    { /* ... */ }
function taxable(reading) { /* ... */ }

name: Split Phase
tradeoff: An intermediate data structure between the phases is overhead — earn it by separating two clearly different concerns.
goal: Each phase reads and writes its own well-defined inputs and outputs; the seam between them is data, not control flow.
savings: Phases evolve independently; tests target each phase in isolation; the intermediate shape becomes a documented contract.
after:
function pricing(input) { return { ...input, price: computePrice(input) }; }
function render(priced)  { return renderHTML(priced); }

name: Move Function
tradeoff: Moving a function across modules can pull dependencies with it — confirm the new home actually has access to everything the function needs.
goal: Each function lives where its data lives; coupling between modules drops.
savings: Modules become more cohesive; tests stay focused; feature-envy patterns disappear.
before: class Order { totalPriority() { return this.account.priority(); } }
after:
class Account { priority() { /* ... */ } }
class Order   { /* asks account directly when needed */ }

name: Move Field
tradeoff: Moving a field disturbs every reader — refactor in tooling-supported steps and add a temporary accessor on the original class while migrating.
goal: Each field belongs to the class that owns its lifecycle; cross-class reaching disappears.
savings: Class boundaries align with data ownership; mutations are local; refactoring becomes safer.
before: class Customer { plan; discountRate; }
after:
class Plan     { discountRate; }
class Customer { plan; /* discountRate accessed via plan */ }

name: Slide Statements
tradeoff: Reordering can change behavior if statements aren't actually independent — verify side effects and dependencies before sliding.
goal: Related statements sit next to each other; the function reads as a sequence of cohesive sub-steps that are easy to extract.
savings: Setup for Extract Function becomes trivial; the implicit grouping inside the function becomes explicit.

name: Split Loop
tradeoff: Two loops over the same collection are slower than one — only split when the doubled cost is dwarfed by the readability gain (which it usually is).
goal: Each loop does one thing; mixed-purpose loops separate into named single-purpose passes.
savings: Each loop can then be replaced by a pipeline or extracted by name; bugs concentrate in one purpose at a time.
after:
const totalSalary = people.reduce((s, p) => s + p.salary, 0);
const youngest    = Math.min(...people.map(p => p.age));

name: Replace Loop with Pipeline
tradeoff: Pipelines add a tiny per-element function-call overhead — usually negligible, but profile if you're in a hot path.
goal: Filter / map / reduce expresses the transformation as a sequence of named operations; intent jumps off the page.
savings: Off-by-one and accumulator bugs vanish; each step is independently testable.

name: Remove Dead Code
tradeoff: Code that looks dead may be reachable via reflection, dynamic dispatch, or external callers — delete in version control where it can be recovered.
goal: Every line in the codebase is reachable and used; readers don't waste cycles on phantom branches.
savings: Smaller surface, faster reading, fewer false leads when debugging.
before:
function legacyDiscount(order) { /* unused since 2018 */ }
function modernDiscount(order) { /* the real one */ }
after: function discount(order) { /* the real one */ }

name: Split Variable
tradeoff: Two distinct uses of one variable share a single update pattern that may have hidden coupling — verify each use is genuinely independent.
goal: Each variable has one role; reassignment patterns reflect distinct purposes rather than reused storage.
savings: Names match purpose; the type system can narrow each role; refactoring each use becomes local.

name: Rename Field
tradeoff: Field renames cross every reader/writer of the class — refactor in tooling-supported steps and update tests with each batch.
goal: Field names match the domain role they play; readers don't need to inspect usage to know what a field means.
savings: Stronger encapsulation; future-you reads the class definition and immediately understands its shape.
before: class Org { name; }
after: class Org { title; }

name: Replace Derived Variable with Query
tradeoff: If the derivation is expensive and the source rarely changes, recomputing on every read may be wasteful — measure before deciding.
goal: Values computed from other state are computed on demand; no separate field needs to be kept in sync.
savings: Mutation scope shrinks; reasoning about state is simpler; no chance of the derived field drifting from its source.

name: Decompose Conditional
tradeoff: Names that aren't crisper than the underlying condition add ceremony — only extract when the named function/variable says something the condition can't.
goal: Conditions and their consequents read as named domain decisions: isInSummer(), discountFor(date), etc.
savings: The branching logic reads top-to-bottom as a story; bugs concentrate in the named pieces.

name: Consolidate Conditional Expression
tradeoff: Combining conditions can hide their independent reasons — only consolidate when they truly express the same business rule.
goal: Multiple conditions leading to the same action collapse into one named predicate.
savings: The shared rationale becomes visible and namable; new conditions extend one place instead of N.
after: if (isIneligibleForBonus(employee)) return 0;

name: Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses
tradeoff: If multiple paths share work, premature returns can duplicate that work — extract first, then guard.
goal: Edge cases bail out early at the top of the function; the main flow is unindented and tells the happy path linearly.
savings: Indentation drops; the dominant case is obvious; new edge cases land at the top without disturbing the rest.

name: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
tradeoff: If only one switch on the type code exists, polymorphism is overkill — wait for the second or third repeat before extracting subclasses.
goal: Each case becomes a class implementing a shared interface; dispatch happens once via virtual call.
savings: Adding a new case is one new class; the type system tells you what's missing.
after: event.handle(); // ClickEvent and KeyEvent each implement handle()

name: Introduce Special Case
tradeoff: Adds a tiny class for one case; only worthwhile when the special case appears in 2+ consumers.
goal: A repeating null-or-special check becomes a Null Object (or Special Case) that responds sensibly to the same interface.
savings: Callers stop branching on identity; the special behavior lives in one place.
before: const name = customer === 'unknown' ? 'occupant' : customer.name;
after: const name = customer.name; // UnknownCustomer.name returns 'occupant'

name: Introduce Assertion
tradeoff: Assertions used as control flow couple production behavior to debug-mode invariants — keep them as runtime contracts that should never fire.
goal: Invariants the code assumes are stated explicitly; readers don't need to deduce them.
savings: Bugs that violate the invariant fail loudly at the source instead of bubbling out as mysterious downstream errors.
before:
// rate must be positive
const tax = base * rate;
after:
if (rate <= 0) throw new Error('rate must be positive');
const tax = base * rate;

name: Separate Query from Modifier
tradeoff: If the modification and the query truly cannot be separated (e.g. find-and-remove on a queue), the constraint is fundamental — leave the combined operation but document it.
goal: Functions either return a value or mutate state, never both — callers can compose them without surprise.
savings: Reasoning about side effects is local; tests target each shape independently.

name: Parameterize Function
tradeoff: If the variations are conceptually different operations, one parameterized function will accumulate flags and special cases — keep them separate then.
goal: Two near-identical functions that differ only in literal values combine into one with a parameter.
savings: One canonical implementation; new variations are new parameter values, not new functions.
before:
function tenPercentRaise(person)  { person.salary *= 1.10; }
function fivePercentRaise(person) { person.salary *= 1.05; }
after: function raise(person, factor) { person.salary *= 1 + factor; }

name: Remove Flag Argument
tradeoff: Two replacement functions with similar bodies introduce duplication — pair this with Extract Function for shared internals.
goal: Each flag value becomes its own well-named function; callers say what they mean rather than passing booleans.
savings: Call sites read fluently; new variations land as new functions instead of new switch cases.
after:
function setHeight(value) { /* ... */ }
function setWidth(value)  { /* ... */ }

name: Preserve Whole Object
tradeoff: Passing the whole object adds coupling to its full surface — only do this when the called function might reasonably need other parts of the object.
goal: Instead of pulling several values out of an object to pass them in, pass the object itself.
savings: Signatures shrink; adding a needed field is internal; consumers don't have to plumb new arguments through.
before: if (room.lowTemp < range.low || room.highTemp > range.high) { /* ... */ }
after: if (range.includes(room)) { /* ... */ }

name: Replace Parameter with Query
tradeoff: If the query has side effects or is expensive, passing the value is genuinely better — only replace when the query is pure and cheap.
goal: When a function can compute its own answer from already-available state, callers don't have to pre-compute it.
savings: Signatures shrink; consumers stop doing the function's homework.
after: const final = discounted(order); // computes basePrice and level itself

name: Replace Constructor with Factory Function
tradeoff: Hides the actual class from callers — make sure your factory's name still expresses the produced shape clearly.
goal: Object creation goes through a named function that can validate, choose subclasses, or return cached instances.
savings: Construction can vary per case; consumers don't depend on which concrete class they're getting.
before: const employee = new Employee(name, 'engineer', salary);

name: Pull Up Method
tradeoff: If the methods only superficially resemble each other, pulling up creates a fake-shared abstraction — unify only when behavior is actually identical.
goal: Methods that subclasses implement identically move to the shared superclass.
savings: One implementation, one place to fix; subclasses focus on what's actually different.
before:
class Manager  extends Employee { name() { return this._name; } }
class Engineer extends Employee { name() { return this._name; } }

name: Push Down Method
tradeoff: If the method is occasionally needed in the parent, pushing it down forces awkward type checks back at consumers — verify usage first.
goal: Methods used by only one subclass live with that subclass, not on the shared superclass.
savings: The superclass surface shrinks; subclasses that don't need the method aren't burdened by it.

name: Replace Type Code with Subclasses
tradeoff: If only one or two switches exist on the type code, subclassing is over-design; combine with Replace Conditional with Polymorphism only when dispatch repeats.
goal: A 'kind' string field becomes a real subclass type; the type system enforces the legal set.
savings: Compile-time checks that no kind is missed; per-kind behavior lives where it belongs.

name: Extract Superclass
tradeoff: Inheritance is inflexible — if the duplication is shallow, prefer Extract Class (composition) over Extract Superclass.
goal: Two classes with substantial shared structure get a common parent that owns the shared bits.
savings: Bug fixes and new shared behavior land in one place; the relationship between the classes is documented in code.
before:
class Employee   { name; id; salary; }
class Department { name; id; budget; }

name: Collapse Hierarchy
tradeoff: Collapsing too eagerly destroys an extension point you'll later want — only collapse when the variant has been zero-sum for a sustained period.
goal: A subclass that no longer differs meaningfully from its parent merges back in.
savings: Smaller hierarchy, less ceremony, fewer files to navigate.
before:
class Employee {}
class FullTimeEmployee extends Employee {}
after: class Employee {}

name: Replace Subclass with Delegate
tradeoff: Composition is more verbose at construction sites — accept the verbosity in exchange for the flexibility.
goal: Behavior that varied via inheritance now varies via a delegate object that implements the variant interface.
savings: Variants can be combined or swapped at runtime; Liskov violations vanish; the hierarchy tree flattens.

name: Extract Class
tradeoff: Premature class extraction adds ceremony — extract when 3+ fields and at least one operation cluster around a single concept that the parent class doesn't own.
goal: A cohesive sub-concept inside a class becomes its own class with its own name, fields, and methods.
savings: Each class has one purpose; tests target the small unit; the parent class shrinks.

name: Replace Primitive with Object
tradeoff: Wrapping every primitive is overkill — wrap when the concept needs validation, formatting, or domain-specific behavior beyond what the primitive offers.
goal: Each domain concept has a small typed home — Money, PhoneNumber, OrderId — that knows its rules.
savings: Misuse becomes a type error; behavior accretes around the concept; refactoring is local to the wrapper.

name: Hide Delegate
tradeoff: Adds a passthrough method on the parent for every delegated operation — only worth it for operations that are repeated across consumers.
goal: Callers ask the closest object for what they want; the object delegates internally without exposing its collaborators.
savings: Encapsulation tightens; intermediate objects can change shape without breaking callers.
before: const street = order.customer.address.street;
after:
// inside Order: customerStreet() { return this.customer.address.street; }
const street = order.customerStreet();

name: Remove Middle Man
tradeoff: Direct access to the delegate exposes its surface to every consumer — only remove the middle man when most of its methods are passthroughs.
goal: Callers talk directly to the real object; trivial passthroughs are deleted.
savings: Fewer files, shorter call stacks, the implementation's location is obvious.
after:
// Expose team directly when the wrapper adds nothing.
manager.team.members();

name: Replace Magic Literal
tradeoff: Naming every literal can drown the file in trivia — only name literals that carry domain meaning the surrounding code can't speak.
goal: Bare numbers and strings that encode domain concepts become named constants whose name says what the value represents.
savings: Searches by domain term find every callsite; changing the value is one edit; the constant invites code-side documentation when it's truly load-bearing.

name: Move Statements into Function
tradeoff: If the moved statements aren't always wanted, the function grows a flag argument — verify every caller really needs the moved behavior.
goal: Setup or follow-up that happens around every call to a function moves inside the function, so the caller's contract shrinks.
savings: One fewer thing to remember at the call site; consistency is enforced by the function's definition, not by convention.

name: Move Statements to Callers
tradeoff: If most callers want the moved statements, you've created duplication — the inverse of Move Statements into Function is only an improvement when callers genuinely differ.
goal: Statements that vary by caller move out of the function so each caller chooses its own setup or follow-up.
savings: The function's body becomes about its single responsibility; callers express their differences directly.

name: Replace Inline Code with Function Call
tradeoff: If the existing function's name doesn't quite match the local intent, the call site reads as a near-miss; consider Change Function Declaration first.
goal: When inline code reproduces what a named function already does, the inline copy is replaced by a call.
savings: One canonical implementation; the name labels the intent; future improvements to the function reach every site that used to inline.
before: const inRange = candidate >= low && candidate <= high;
after: const inRange = between(candidate, low, high);

name: Replace Temp with Query
tradeoff: If the temp wraps an expensive calculation called many times, naive replacement may multiply cost — measure or cache before deciding.
goal: A local variable assigned once from a computation becomes a function that returns that computation on demand.
savings: Extract Function becomes easier (the query has a name and stable scope); the temp's lifetime no longer constrains how the surrounding function is split.

name: Replace Function with Command
tradeoff: Promoting a function to a command adds ceremony (constructor, method calls). Only worth it when the function genuinely needs its own intermediate state or multiple entry points.
goal: A function with rich internal state becomes an object whose methods can share that state — easier to extract, name, and test in pieces.
savings: Long sequences become labeled steps; tests target each step on the command; subclasses or strategies can vary parts of the algorithm.

name: Replace Command with Function
tradeoff: If the command holds genuinely useful intermediate state, flattening to a function regrows the temps it eliminated — confirm there's no real reuse first.
goal: A command object whose execute() does everything in one shot collapses back to a plain function.
savings: Fewer files, fewer constructors, less indirection — the caller sees one function instead of build-then-execute.
after:
function charge(c, o) { return c.base + o.tax; }
charge(c, o);

name: Return Modified Value
tradeoff: Callers must remember to capture the returned value; if any forget, they keep the unmodified original. Mark the parameter readonly so the type system helps.
goal: Instead of mutating a parameter in place, the function returns the modified value so the caller reassigns.
savings: Side effects on inputs disappear; the function reads as a transformation; equality and snapshotting become possible.

name: Substitute Algorithm
tradeoff: Swapping algorithms wholesale forfeits behavioral safety — characterize the function with tests at every input boundary you care about before substituting.
goal: An opaque or convoluted algorithm gets replaced by a clearer one (often from a library or well-known pattern) that produces the same outputs.
savings: Future maintainers read the well-known pattern instead of decoding the bespoke implementation; performance and correctness usually improve.

name: Encapsulate Collection
tradeoff: Returning a shallow copy on every read can hide bugs where callers expected mutation to be reflected — be explicit about the contract.
goal: A class's internal collection is never returned directly; callers add or remove via methods on the class, and reads return a snapshot or iterator.
savings: The owner can enforce invariants (uniqueness, ordering, max size); refactoring the collection's internal shape is local.

name: Encapsulate Record
tradeoff: Wrapping every record adds ceremony — only worth it when behavior or validation will accrete around the data.
goal: A bare record (plain object with public fields) becomes a class whose properties are accessed through methods that can validate, log, or derive.
savings: Field renames stay internal; invariants can be enforced on every read or write; the record becomes a real domain object.
before:
const org = { name: 'Acme', country: 'US' };
console.log(org.name);

name: Remove Setting Method
tradeoff: Removing a setter forces every legitimate update through a more meaningful method — verify there's a domain action behind every setter call before deleting it.
goal: Fields whose values should only be set at construction lose their setters; callers either construct a new object or call a domain method that changes the field as a side effect of doing real work.
savings: Immutable-by-default classes; bugs from late mutation vanish; the API expresses what users can actually do.

name: Inline Class
tradeoff: If the absorbing class was already large, inlining piles more onto it — fold in only when the absorber stays under its complexity budget afterward.
goal: A class with too few responsibilities to deserve its own file folds into a class it collaborates with most.
savings: Fewer files, fewer constructors, shorter call paths; the absorbing class's coherence improves when it gains the methods it was already orchestrating.

name: Change Reference to Value
tradeoff: Comparison semantics shift from identity to equality — every call site that depended on `===` or identity caches needs review.
goal: An object treated as a sharable record (with setters) becomes a value object — immutable, equal by content, replaced rather than mutated.
savings: Concurrency hazards disappear; the type system can mark fields readonly; the object can travel safely across boundaries.

name: Change Value to Reference
tradeoff: Sharing introduces the question 'who owns this?' — make sure the lifetime and visibility of the shared reference are well-defined.
goal: Duplicate copies of a logically-single entity collapse into one shared object that everyone references.
savings: Updates to the entity are visible everywhere; storage shrinks; identity becomes meaningful again.
before:
// every order carries its own Customer copy
orders.forEach(o => o.customer = { name: 'Acme' });
after:
const acme = customerRepository.find('Acme');
orders.forEach(o => o.customer = acme);

name: Replace Control Flag with Break
tradeoff: If the loop body is large, the break can hide the early-exit semantics — extract a function around the loop's body to keep the exit obvious.
goal: Loops that maintain a boolean to decide when to stop replace it with a direct `break`, `return`, or `continue`.
savings: The exit condition appears at the moment it's decided, not as a delayed effect of a flag check; the loop's intent becomes literal.

name: Replace Query with Parameter
tradeoff: Passing the value pushes the responsibility onto callers; for many call sites, signatures grow noisily — prefer this when the query touches global or volatile state.
goal: A function that reads from a query (global, singleton, instance state) instead accepts the value as a parameter and becomes referentially transparent.
savings: The function becomes testable in isolation; its dependencies are visible in its signature; pure-function reasoning becomes possible.

name: Replace Error Code with Exception
tradeoff: Exceptions for predictable conditions misuse the mechanism — only convert codes that represent genuine, exceptional, unrecoverable failures.
goal: Numeric or string error codes that callers must remember to check are replaced with exceptions that propagate by default.
savings: Forgetting to check no longer silently swallows the error; the type system marks the failure path; cleanup happens via finally / try-with.

name: Replace Exception with Precheck
tradeoff: Race conditions: the precheck may pass and the operation still fail (TOCTOU). Use prechecks only for conditions the caller can verify without a race.
goal: Exceptions used for predictable, checkable conditions become an explicit precheck the caller can perform, leaving exceptions for truly exceptional cases.
savings: The error path is local and visible; reading code top-to-bottom describes the rules rather than the failure response; debuggers stop catching benign throws.
after:
if (i >= amounts.length) return 0;
return amounts[i] / 100;

name: Pull Up Constructor Body
tradeoff: If only some subclasses share the init logic, pulling it up forces the others to opt out — verify the body is genuinely common.
goal: Initialization code repeated across subclass constructors moves into the parent class's constructor and is called via super.
savings: One canonical home for parent-state init; new subclasses inherit the setup for free; bug fixes apply uniformly.
before:
class Manager  extends Employee { constructor(n, s) { this.name = n; this.salary = s; } }
class Engineer extends Employee { constructor(n, s) { this.name = n; this.salary = s; } }

name: Pull Up Field
tradeoff: Pulling up a field that subclasses use differently (different default, different visibility) creates surprise — verify the field semantics are identical.
goal: A field declared identically in two or more subclasses moves to the shared superclass.
savings: One source of truth for the field's type and default; subclasses focus on what they actually specialize.
before:
class Manager  extends Employee { _name; }
class Engineer extends Employee { _name; }

name: Push Down Field
tradeoff: If the field is occasionally consulted in the parent for type checks, pushing it down forces awkward downcasts — verify usage first.
goal: A field used by only one subclass moves out of the parent and into that subclass.
savings: Other subclasses no longer carry storage they ignore; the parent's surface shrinks; the field's meaning becomes local.
after:
class Employee {}
class Salesperson extends Employee { quota; }

name: Remove Subclass
tradeoff: Removing a subclass referenced by name elsewhere (factories, registries) breaks those references — confirm no consumer is type-testing the subclass.
goal: A subclass whose only purpose was to encode a type code or add nothing collapses back into a field on the parent.
savings: Smaller hierarchy; new variants are field values instead of new files; the parent regains its variability point as data.

name: Replace Superclass with Delegate
tradeoff: Adds a forwarding method on the former subclass for every method the old superclass exposed — only worth it when the superclass relationship is misleading.
goal: Inheritance from a superclass that doesn't really fit (Liskov violations, awkward methods) becomes composition: the former subclass holds an instance and delegates explicitly.
savings: The misleading is-a relationship disappears; the former subclass can change its delegate's class without affecting its callers.
